questions.q: Why does this case study treat direct consumers and repair-shop partners as two separate identity designs?
options: Because consumers never need any Salesforce access at all
Because partners should always be treated as internal employees
Because Salesforce technically cannot support two populations in one org
Because they have fundamentally different needs — consumers need low-friction self-registration, while partners need bounded, role-based, admin-approved access with delegated administration
questions.explain: Consumers are a CIAM population prioritizing low friction, while partners are a bounded population needing persistent role-based access and delegated administration — treating them identically would poorly serve one or both groups.

questions.q: What design pattern resolves the tension between minimizing signup friction and confirming identity before showing sensitive order data?
options: Progressive profiling — minimal friction at signup, with stronger identity checks required only at the specific moment sensitive data or actions are requested
Removing all authentication requirements entirely
Using delegated authentication instead of SSO
Requiring full identity verification at initial signup for every user
questions.explain: Progressive profiling lets signup stay low-friction while requiring additional identity confidence (like confirming an order number) only when the user tries to access something sensitive.

questions.q: Why should repair-shop partners self-register the same way consumers do?
options: Partners should always use delegated authentication instead of Experience Cloud
They should — self-registration is equally appropriate for both
They generally should NOT self-register; partner relationships are typically admin-approved, with delegated administration for managing their own technicians
Repair shops cannot be given Experience Cloud access at all
questions.explain: Partner relationships are established business relationships, not anonymous signups, so admin-approved onboarding with delegated administration is the appropriate pattern rather than open self-registration.

questions.q: How does a repair-shop technician's required data visibility differ structurally from a typical consumer's?
options: Technicians should see every Account in the org with no restriction
Consumers need broader visibility than technicians
They are identical; both should see only their own Account's records
A technician needs visibility spanning multiple customer Accounts (whichever customers their shop services), while a consumer's visibility is scoped to just their own Account
questions.explain: A repair-shop technician's sharing needs span multiple customer Accounts serviced by their shop, which is structurally different from a single consumer's visibility scoped to their own Account alone — this needs explicit sharing-rule design.

questions.q: What's the key architectural skill this case study is meant to illustrate?
options: Recognizing when a stated requirement ('a portal') is actually two different requirements with opposing priorities, and designing for each explicitly
That self-registration should never be used in Experience Cloud
That partner identity is identical to workforce identity
That every portal request should use exactly one identity pattern regardless of population
questions.explain: The case study's core lesson is recognizing mixed populations hiding inside one stated requirement, and designing distinct identity treatments for each rather than forcing a single pattern onto both.
